name: Svetlana Kitić
milestone_by_age_26: Named the world's best young female handball player in 1977 at age 17, and won Olympic silver medal at the 1980 Moscow Olympics at age 20.
early_history_summary: Kitić grew up in a working-class family in Tuzla, Bosnia, and began playing handball at age 14 for Jedinstvo Tuzla. At 15, she moved alone to Belgrade to join Radnički, where she trained intensively and was called to the Yugoslav national team at 16. By 17, she was named the world's best young player, and by 20 she had an Olympic silver medal and a European Champions Cup title.
family_context_summary: Born into a working-class family in Tuzla; her father was a safety engineer at a mine and her mother was a homemaker. The family lived modestly on a single salary.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite club pipeline, early specialization, national team at 16, working-class origin
evidence_summary: Kitić emerged from a working-class Bosnian family to become a handball prodigy, moving to Belgrade at 15 to join Radnički's elite club system. She was called to the Yugoslav national team at 16 and named the world's best young player at 17, reflecting deep early specialization and access to Yugoslavia's top handball pipeline. Her father was a mine safety engineer and her mother a homemaker; no family domain advantage in sports is documented. The Yugoslav sports system provided the elite institutional pipeline that concentrated opportunity for her.
starting_point: Born into a working-class family in Tuzla, Bosnia; father was a mine safety engineer and mother a homemaker, living modestly on a single salary.
current_position: Retired from competitive handball; resides in Belgrade; voted best female handball player of all time by the IHF in 2010; later served as a member of parliament in Serbia.

name: Alexis Argüello
milestone_by_age_26: Won the WBA featherweight world championship on November 23, 1974 at age 22 by knocking out Ruben Olivares in the 13th round in Los Angeles.
early_history_summary: Argüello grew up in abject poverty in Managua, Nicaragua, where his father was a shoemaker. He left school at 12, worked on a dairy farm at 9, and spent a year in Canada at 13 to support his family. He compiled a 58-2 amateur record before turning professional at 16 in 1968, and won 29 of his next 30 bouts to earn a world title shot.
family_context_summary: Born into abject poverty in Managua; father was a shoemaker who attempted suicide when Alexis was 5. One of eight children. Left school at 12 and worked to support the family.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family boxing background; Argüello took up boxing after his sister married a boxer. His father was a shoemaker.
primary_early_advantage_tags: poverty, early pro debut at 16, amateur record 58-2, trainer Miguel Angel Rivas, physical talent
evidence_summary: Argüello rose from extreme poverty in Managua, turning professional at 16 after a brief amateur career (58-2). His father was a shoemaker and the family lived in one of Managua's worst neighborhoods. He was trained by Miguel Angel Rivas and overcame early losses to win 29 of 30 bouts, earning a world title shot at 22. His unusual height and reach for a featherweight gave him natural physical advantages. The adversity of his upbringing created the urgency that drove his boxing career.
starting_point: Born into abject poverty in Managua, Nicaragua; father was a shoemaker, mother a homemaker; one of eight children in one of the city's worst neighborhoods.
current_position: Died on July 1, 2009 at age 57 in Managua; final role: Mayor of Managua, elected in 2008; three-division world champion and International Boxing Hall of Fame inductee.

By 17, he had invented two skills bearing his name, and at 18 he became European champion on horizontal bar.

He progressed through Jokerit's ranks to the senior club at 17, won European Junior gold at 18, and was drafted by the Edmonton Oilers in 1980. The Edmonton Oilers dynasty of the 1980s represented a structural wave in NHL hockey, and Kurri was a central figure in winning five Stanley Cups.
